# Experimental design

## Models, prompts, and inference

We study pretrained Gemma 3 270M and 1B [@gemma3]. Sparse experiments use the matching
Gemma Scope 2 pretrained affine cross-layer transcoders
[@gemmascope2], building on transcoder feature-circuit methods
[@dunefsky2024transcoders; @ameisen2025attribution], through `circuit-tracer`
[@hanna2025circuittracer] and NNsight [@fiotto2025nnsight]. The primary
prompts and occupation definitions follow the released materials of *Latent
Planning Emerges with Scale* [@hanna2026latent]; synonym families are screened
from the same occupation domain. Appendix A.1 records model, dictionary, and
package snapshots and maps each claim to its frozen configuration and
machine-readable result artifact.

Unless stated otherwise, we recompute the full prompt with caching disabled,
use bfloat16 model inference, and measure full-vocabulary next-token
distributions. Sparse interventions multiply prompt-specific feature
activations at the pre-article position. Residual interventions add a
source-to-target direction at a specified decoder layer. Development prompts
select features, layers, or strengths; headline estimates use disjoint held-out
prompts or leave-one-semantic-family-out selection. Intervals are 10,000-sample
prompt- or family-bootstrap 95% intervals. Exact paired sign and sign-flip tests,
or independent-group label permutations, are used where family counts permit.

## Public endpoint: the sparse S1 intervention

At 270M, attribution graphs on eight selection occupations nominate four S1
features with positive article and future-noun paths. The feature set is frozen
before evaluation on 20 held-out occupations and amplified \(5\times\). We run
the six cells, then two direct falsification tests: **phenocopy**, which replays
the treated article with S1 off, and **rescue**, which restores the baseline
article while S1 remains on. A prompt-aligned binary search brackets each
article argmax transition and compares free and fixed-article noun distributions
over the same gain interval. Float32 final-head and stochastic-policy audits
test whether the conclusion depends on bfloat16 logits or greedy decoding.

## Private-route references

To establish that later nouns remain sensitive to upstream state after article
identity is fixed, we patch natural-state-derived residual directions at the
pre-article position. Source and target states come from occupation descriptions
that do not name the tested noun. A pooled development sweep selects a layer;
held-out target patches are compared with wrong-target, sign-reversed, and
matched-norm random controls. We run the same normalized construction at 270M
and 1B. These are target-directed full-residual capacity interventions, not a
claim that the sparse S1 features naturally carry the same state.

## Neutral synonym routing assay

The mediator-relative test uses six cross-article and eight within-article
occupation-synonym families. For example, `teacher`/`educator` cross article
classes, whereas `doctor`/`physician` do not. Both alternatives correctly answer
one occupational definition. The evaluated prompt contains an unrelated
occupation-format demonstration followed by the neutral definition; it contains
neither tested synonym nor a first-letter instruction. Explicit donor prompts
name each source or target word and define

$$
\delta=h_{\rm target}^{(\ell)}-h_{\rm source}^{(\ell)},\qquad
h_{\rm eval}^{(\ell)}\leftarrow h_{\rm eval}^{(\ell)}+s\delta.
$$

Leave-one-family-out selection chooses layer 17/25 in every fold. The primary
setting is native strength \(s=1\) and article-policy temperature \(\tau=1\),
with \(s\in\{0.5,1,1.5\}\) and
\(\tau\in\{0.1,0.25,0.5,1\}\) as robustness checks. Before route inference we
require positive held-out target-minus-source movement and high retained
`a/an` policy mass. Controls use a wrong target and the reversed direction.

For each family we project public and private probability vectors onto the
intended target-minus-source contrast. Let \(P\) and \(H\) denote the signed
public and fixed-token private effects, respectively, and define route contrast
\(R=P-H\). Cross-class families predict
\(R>0\); within-class families predict \(R<0\). The interaction compares the two
groups, while exact within-family sign flips test each simple effect separately.

Before any model or route measurement, we semantically curated and froze 22
candidate triads whose three words were intended as valid alternatives for one definition.
The repaired matched-triad test holds semantic family, definition, source word,
source donor, and evaluated prompt fixed while comparing one same-article and
one cross-article target. Its route-blind admissibility screen uses only
single-token lexical realization, positive fixed-target-article local efficacy,
and retained article support. The prespecified paired estimand is
\(R_{\rm cross}-R_{\rm within}\), tested by a paired semantic-family bootstrap,
an exact one-sided binomial sign test, and an exact paired sign-flip randomization
test. Fourteen of 22 frozen candidate triads
pass the screen, exceeding the minimum gate of eight.

## Closed-loop gain prediction

For 32 sparse features selected on disjoint occupations, attribution is
calibrated to intervention-induced article-margin movement. Equation 1 then
combines predicted movement with intervention-off decoder susceptibility and
fixed-branch continuation leverage. We compare constant, attribution-only,
susceptibility-only, leverage-only, activation-magnitude, and constant-shift
baselines. Combined feature-and-prompt holdout excludes both identities from the
calibration fold while permitting intervention-off quantities for the held-out
prompt. A measured-margin version is reported only as an accounting oracle.
